extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of English common law (law students, lawyers, judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the nature, kinds, creation, incidents, privileges, disabilities, visitation, duties, and dissolution of corporations under English common law (Blackstone's Commentaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and definition of corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: Artificial persons (bodies politic, bodies corporate) constituted to maintain perpetual succession and enjoy a kind of legal immortality, for the advantage of the public where particular rights should be kept on foot and continued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains advantages with example of a college: corporations enable continuing rules, coercive power, defence of privileges, and continuity of property without endless conveyances; compares corporate identity to the river Thames (same river though parts change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into aggregate and sole corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate corporations consist of many persons united into one society with perpetual succession; sole corporations consist of one person and his successors (incorporated in a particular station).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aggregate — mayor and commonalty, head and fellows of a college; sole — the king, bishops, parsons and vicars. Notes different practical incidents (e.g., moveable property and seals less relevant to sole corporations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division into ecclesiastical and lay corporations (and civil vs eleemosynary lay bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ecclesiastical corporations are composed of spiritual persons (bishops, deans, chapters); lay corporations are civil (temporal purposes) or eleemosynary (charitable endowments for perpetual distribution of alms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives examples (churchwardens, college of physicians, hospitals, university colleges), and explains that eleemosynary corporations, though sometimes composed of clergy, are legally lay bodies with particular rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: King's consent necessary for creation
rubrics_metrics.description: In England the king's consent (implied or express) is absolutely necessary to the erection of any corporation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creation may be by common law (implied consent), by prescription, by act of parliament, or by the king's letters patent/charter; common-law corporations include those 'virtute officii' (e.g., king, bishops).

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation by prescription or common law
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations may exist by virtue of common law or prescription where consent is implied (e.g., ancient towns like the city of London; bodies whose existence 'time whereof the memory of man runneth not to the contrary').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where charters are lost through antiquity, law presumes a charter once existed; such bodies are regarded as well created despite lack of extant charter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation by act of parliament or letters patent/charter
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations may be created expressly by statute or commonly by the king's letters patent using words like 'creamus, erigimus, fundamus, incorporamus', and grants such as 'gildam mercatoriam' may suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many statutes either confirm prior royal charters or empower future incorporation (examples: college of physicians, Bank of England). The king may also grant a subject power to erect corporations (qui facit per alium, facit per se).

rubrics_metrics.name: Name of the corporation is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: When a corporation is erected, a name must be given it; by that name alone it must sue and be sued and do all legal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name is 'the very being of its constitution' — likened to baptism: slight variations immaterial, but the corporate name is the knot of its combination and necessary for corporate functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inseparable incidents of every (aggregate) corporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain powers are tacitly annexed at incorporation: (1) perpetual succession; (2) to sue or be sued, implead or be impleaded, grant or receive, by its corporate name; (3) to purchase lands and hold them for itself and successors; (4) to have a common seal; (5) to make by-laws for its own government (unless contrary to law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These five are treated as necessarily incident, especially to aggregate corporations; two (seal and statutes) are less necessary for sole corporations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate acts manifested by common seal
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation, being an invisible body, acts only by its common seal; the fixing of the seal unites the several assents of the individuals and makes one joint assent of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private signatures or words of members do not bind the corporation — the seal evidences corporate intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to make by-laws and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations may make by-laws or private statutes for their own government which are binding unless contrary to the law of the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: Roman law tolerated internal rules so long as not contrary to public law. Exception for trading companies: cannot make by-laws affecting the king's prerogative or common profit without judicial/chancellor approval (Stat. 19 Hen. VII c.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Must appear by attorney; inability to appear in person
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation must always appear by attorney and cannot appear in person because it is 'invisible' and exists only in legal contemplation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequent procedural differences: proceedings to compel a corporation to appear are by distress on lands and goods; it cannot be personally arrested or imprisoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate incapacity for corporal crimes and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation cannot commit treason or felony or other crimes in its corporate capacity, nor is it capable of suffering corporal punishments, attainder, forfeiture, or corruption of blood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members can commit crimes in their individual capacities; civil law likewise treated directors as personally answerable in certain misbehaviours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to perform certain personal offices and trusts
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation cannot be executor or administrator, cannot take an oath for personal office execution, cannot be a trustee in the sense of personal confidence, and cannot be committed to prison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of these disabilities, the law treats certain trusts and personal duties as unsuitable for corporations; remedies against a corporation differ (distress rather than imprisonment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immunity from excommunication and outlawry
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation cannot be excommunicated and is not liable to be summoned into ecclesiastical courts; it cannot be outlawed because outlawry presupposes a possible arrest which a corporation cannot suffer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blackstone observes corporations have 'no soul' and thus ecclesiastical censures do not reach them; this has implications for jurisdiction and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate-specific powers and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate corporations may take goods and chattels for benefit of themselves and successors; may have a head (dean, warden) whose vacancy restricts corporate acts except appointing another; act of majority is act of whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moveables are unsuitable for sole corporations due to risk of loss/embezzlement and disputes. On majority rule: Roman law required two-thirds, but English law treats any majority as sufficient; Stat. 33 Hen. VIII c.27 made void private statutes that allowed a minority to obstruct grants or elections made by head with concurrence of majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to purchase lands and statutes of mortmain
rubrics_metrics.description: At common law corporations have capacity to purchase lands for themselves and successors, but are excepted out of the statute of wills (no devise by will good, except charitable uses) and their power to purchase from living grantors is curtailed by statutes of mortmain requiring royal licence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mortmain statutes (from Magna Carta through later Acts) restrict and require licences; Blackstone defers detailed exposition but notes these statutory incapacities and the need for licence in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: General duty of corporations
rubrics_metrics.description: The general duties of all bodies politic, in corporate capacity, reduce to a single one: to act up to the end or design for which they were created by their founder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is analogous to duties of natural persons — corporate governance should pursue founding purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visitation: who may visit corporations and forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations are 'visited' (inspected and corrected) by persons appointed by law: ecclesiastical corporations by the ordinary (canon law), lay corporations by the founder, his heirs or assigns; civil corporations' visitation lies in the king's bench (king as founder).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains jurisdictional rules: king's bench is the place for misbehaviour of civil corporations; if founder appoints a visitor, that visitor's decisions are often final (subject to limited review); where no visitor appointed, bishop or ordinary may visit in certain cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eleemosynary visitation rules and founder distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: For eleemosynary corporations the law distinguishes fundatio incipiens (incorporation — king founder) and fundatio perficiens (dotation — donor as founder); the dotator and his heirs are visitors unless founder appoints another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutes modified visitor rights (e.g., 2 Hen. V c.1; 14 Eliz. c.5) — if founder appoints none the bishop may visit; hospitals founded under statute 39 Eliz. c.5 have visitors nominated by founders. Historical cases (Philips and Bury) clarify limits of judicial review of visitor's determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution and reversion of corporate property
rubrics_metrics.description: A corporation may be dissolved (civil death) in several ways; upon dissolution lands and tenements shall revert to the person (or his heirs) who granted them to the corporation because a condition is annexed that if corporation be dissolved the grantor shall have the lands again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual members may be disfranchised or resign; when the corporate body itself is dissolved, the law treats the original grant conditionally so that property returns to grantor/ heirs.
